A2.text:
Orkhan is twenty-six and works in a bank in Baku. Every day he sits at a computer for nine hours. In his leisure time, he only looked at his phone to kill time.

“You need to pick up a hobby,” his aunt Sevda told him. “Find a creative outlet. My friend Fuad makes small wooden ships in his garage. Why don't you visit him?”

Orkhan did not want to get into something difficult, because he was a complete beginner with his hands. Still, on Saturday he went to Fuad's garage.

Fuad was sixty. He did not only build ships; he also loved to collect old chessboards without pieces. “Making the missing pieces is my favourite pastime,” Fuad said. He gave Orkhan a small piece of walnut wood and a knife.

The first horse Orkhan carved looked like a potato. Fuad laughed, and Orkhan laughed too. After two hours, Orkhan was hooked. He went back every weekend. Slowly, his skill set grew, and he became very dedicated.

In the spring, they finished a whole chess set together and took it to the park by the sea. Two old men immediately sat down to play.

Orkhan did not check his phone once that afternoon.

options: A bank worker who learns to carve wooden chess pieces and forgets about his phone
A man who wins a chess tournament in Baku
How to sell old wooden ships online
An argument between Orkhan and his aunt
questions.why: Orkhan visits Fuad's garage, gets hooked on carving chess pieces, and stops looking at his phone.

questions.q: What did Orkhan's first carved horse look like?
questions.why: “The first horse Orkhan carved looked like a potato.”

questions.q: What did Fuad like to collect?
questions.why: “He also loved to collect old chessboards without pieces.”

questions.q: Orkhan already knew a lot about woodwork before he met Fuad.
questions.why: “He was a complete beginner with his hands.”

questions.q: After two hours, Orkhan was “hooked”. What does “hooked” mean?
options: Enjoying it so much that he wanted to keep doing it
questions.why: He loved it and “went back every weekend”.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention that Orkhan did not check his phone at the end?
options: He had lost his phone in the garage
Carving and watching people use his work gave him real satisfaction instead of just killing time
Phones are not allowed in the park
questions.why: At the start he only looked at his phone to kill time; now the finished chess set holds his attention.

B1.text:
For three years after university, Orkhan's life had two rooms: his desk at the bank and the sofa in his flat. Whenever he had a little leisure time on weekday evenings, he scrolled through his phone simply to kill time until Monday came back around.

His aunt Sevda finally lost patience one Sunday afternoon. “You are twenty-six, not eighty,” she said, putting down her teacup. “You need to pick up a hobby — a real creative outlet where you make something with your hands instead of staring at a glass screen. Go and see my neighbour Fuad on Saturday morning.”

Orkhan was reluctant to get into something new; he had never been good at art at school and felt awkward being a beginner at his age. Still, to keep his aunt quiet, he knocked on the green door of Fuad's courtyard workshop.

The room smelled of walnut shavings, glue and strong black tea. Fuad, a retired ship engineer, used his weekends to collect old, incomplete chessboards from flea markets around Baku and carve the missing pieces himself. “It's a quiet pastime, and nobody is in a hurry here,” he told Orkhan, handing him a small block of wood and a sharp chisel.

Orkhan's first knight looked more like a startled sheep than a horse, yet two hours passed without him noticing. By the third Saturday he was completely hooked. Week by week his skill set grew, and even Fuad was surprised by how dedicated the young banker had become.

In April they carried a completed board down to the boulevard and left it on a stone table under the trees. From a bench nearby, Orkhan watched two strangers sit down, admire the knights and begin a game — and realised his phone had been silent in his pocket all afternoon.

questions.q: How does Orkhan's free time change in the story?
options: He quits his job at the bank to sell furniture
He moves from mindless phone scrolling to the quiet satisfaction of woodcarving
He becomes a professional chess player
He starts teaching art to his aunt
questions.why: He goes from scrolling on the sofa to carving chess pieces with Fuad and watching strangers play with them.

questions.q: Why was Orkhan hesitant to start a new activity at first?
options: He felt awkward being a beginner at twenty-six
questions.why: “He had never been good at art at school and felt awkward being a beginner at his age.”

questions.q: Where did Fuad find the old chessboards?
questions.why: He used his weekends to “collect old, incomplete chessboards from flea markets”.

questions.q: Orkhan and Fuad sold the finished chess set to the two strangers on the boulevard.
questions.why: They “left it on a stone table” for people in the park to play with.

questions.q: Aunt Sevda told Orkhan to find a “creative outlet”. What does this mean?
options: A shop that sells cheap tools
A way to express yourself by making or doing something
A better job at the bank
An electrical socket in the workshop
questions.why: She explains it right after: “where you make something with your hands”.

questions.q: Why did Orkhan leave the chessboard on the stone table instead of taking it home?
options: It was too heavy to carry back
He did not like the way the knights looked
The joy was in making something useful that others could enjoy
Fuad told him there was no space in the workshop
questions.why: He sits nearby watching strangers admire the knights and play, forgetting his phone.

B2.text:
By his mid-twenties, Orkhan had mastered the modern art of looking busy while doing nothing at all. After fifty hours a week in a glass office on Nizami Street, he spent his leisure time on the sofa, scrolling through strangers' holidays merely to kill time until Monday morning rescued him from the silence of his flat.

It was his aunt Sevda who finally staged the intervention. “A man who works only with numbers eventually turns into one,” she declared over Sunday breakfast. “You need to pick up a hobby — a proper creative outlet that leaves sawdust on your shoes. Go and see Fuad in the courtyard behind the old bakery. He's expecting you on Saturday at ten.”

Orkhan rarely wanted to get into something he might fail at in front of witnesses; adulthood had made him allergic to feeling like a beginner. Even so, arguing with Aunt Sevda required far more energy than walking downstairs, so at ten o'clock he stepped into a stone garage that smelled of cedar dust, varnish and cardamom tea.

Fuad, a retired marine engineer with calm hands, had a peculiar pastime: he liked to collect orphaned chessboards from antique stalls around the city — boards missing three pawns, a bishop, or a single black rook — and carve replacement pieces by hand. Without a word of theory, he cleared a stool and handed Orkhan a block of walnut and a curved gouge.

Orkhan's first knight resembled a slightly worried potato, yet when he looked up at the clock on the wall, three hours had vanished. By the fourth week he was unmistakably hooked. His banking skill set — patience, steady fingers and an eye for small margins — turned out to suit wood remarkably well, and Fuad noted with quiet respect how dedicated his quiet apprentice had become.

In May they carried their first completed set down to the stone tables on the Baku boulevard and walked ten paces back into the shade. Two pensioners in flat caps sat down almost at once, testing the weight of the knights in their palms before moving the first pawn. Orkhan stood under the pines watching them play, and realised with a small shock that he hadn't touched his phone since breakfast.

questions.q: What is the main theme of the passage?
options: How learning a patient craft restores a young professional's sense of presence
Why traditional board games are disappearing in Baku
How banking skills can be used to start a small business
The difficulty of finding antique furniture in Azerbaijan
questions.why: Carving missing chess pieces replaces Orkhan's empty phone scrolling with absorbed, patient attention.

questions.q: What did Aunt Sevda mean by “A man who works only with numbers eventually turns into one”?
options: Orkhan should ask for a higher salary
Doing only routine office work makes a person dull and mechanical
questions.why: She immediately tells him to pick up a hobby and find a creative outlet.

questions.q: Which quality from Orkhan's job helped him in woodcarving?
options: His patience and eye for small margins
questions.why: “His banking skill set — patience, an eye for small margins — turned out to suit wood remarkably well.”

questions.q: Fuad gave Orkhan a long lecture on the history of woodcarving before letting him touch the tools.
questions.why: “Without a word of theory, he handed Orkhan a block of walnut and a gouge.”

questions.q: Orkhan scrolled through his phone “merely to kill time”. What does “kill time” mean?
options: Fill empty hours while waiting for something else
Plan every minute of the week
questions.why: He wasn't enjoying it; he was just passing the weekend “until Monday rescued him”.

questions.q: Why did the two pensioners test “the weight of the knights in their palms” before playing?
options: They thought the pieces were made of plastic
They appreciated the handmade quality of the carved wood
They wanted to see if the pieces were stolen
They did not know the rules of chess
questions.why: The hand-carved walnut pieces had a heft and craftsmanship worth noticing before the first move.

podcast.title: Is it a cup or a bowl?

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: What do you do in your free time? Guess: who in this episode has forty-three of the same thing — Leyla or Sam?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is hobbies. And Leyla has something to show me.
[laugh] Yes! Look at this cup. I made it myself.
Wow. It's very… round. Is it a cup or a bowl?
It's a cup! I'm a beginner. I started a pottery class two months ago.
Why pottery?
After work I only looked at my phone to kill time. I wanted to get into something new — something with my hands.
And now?
Now I'm completely hooked. Every Saturday morning I'm at the studio, with clay on my face.
[chuckle] It's a good creative outlet. Your job is all spreadsheets.
Exactly. My brain needs a break. What about you, Sam? What's your favourite pastime?
I collect old football shirts. I have forty-three.
Forty-three! Where do you keep them?
In my wardrobe. My normal clothes live in a box under the bed now.
[laugh] That's dedicated. How did it start?
My dad gave me his shirt from 1994. Then I found one at a market, and then another one… and another one.
I think many people want to pick up a hobby, but they say they don't have time.
True. But leisure time doesn't have to be long. Twenty minutes a day is enough.
And a hobby builds a new skill set. My hands are much more patient now. So am I.
And my hands are very good at… folding shirts.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: what hobby would you like to start — and what is stopping you?
Mine is pottery. Leyla, you can teach me. See you next time!
Bye for now!

options: How to make money from a hobby
Hobbies, free time and how to start one
How to stop using your phone
